{"id":33,"answer":"Your saved notes cover two Java-collections topics directly (plus one adjacent generics note). Per your global guidance, here are short bullets and a note on where each part comes from.

From your notes:
- HashMap vs Hashtable (note 23): HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; Hashtable allows neither. HashMap is not synchronized.
- ArrayList vs LinkedList (note 3): ArrayList gives O(1) random access because it is backed by an array; LinkedList is O(n) for get(i) but O(1) insert/remove at the ends. You flagged that you keep mixing these two up for your DSA exam.
- Adjacent, related to the List interface but not really "collections API behavior": generics type erasure (note 4) — List<String> becomes List at runtime, so you cannot do instanceof List<String> or new T[]; that is why generic varargs gives unchecked warnings.

Tiny code-shaped examples:
- Null handling:
  Map<String,Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
  m.put(null, 1);   // allowed
  m.put("a", null); // allowed
  Hashtable<String,Integer> h = new Hashtable<>();
  h.put(null, 1);   // throws NullPointerException

- Access cost:
  List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(); a.get(0);   // O(1)
  List<Integer> l = new LinkedList<>(); l.get(0);  // O(n)

From general knowledge (NOT in your notes — treat as background to verify):
- HashMap/HashSet are O(1) average for get/put/contains, but O(n) worst case with pathological hashing; since Java 8, long-colliding buckets treeify to give O(log n) worst case.
- TreeMap/TreeSet are sorted and give O(log n) for get/put/contains.
- ArrayList add at the end is amortized O(1) (occasional O(n) resize); insert/remove in the middle is O(n) due to shifting.
- LinkedList has higher per-node memory overhead and worse cache locality, which is why ArrayList is usually the default choice.
